Nobody tells you no. They just stop replying, and you file it as a no.

Go back to the day you sent the quote. You'd found the buyer, had the conversation and priced the job. Then you chased once, maybe twice, something urgent landed and the deal slid down the list. Three weeks later it had gone, and nobody could say exactly when.

Your buyer still had the problem. They solved it with someone who kept going. A second message, a third, a fourth, and they happened to be in front of the buyer the week the budget got signed off.

If you run a £2M+ business, that's one of the most expensive habits there is, because the hard work is already done. You didn't lose on merit. You lost in the third week of doing nothing.

Follow up is something you can build once and stop leaving to memory.

'Just checking in' isn't a follow up. Here's what one should sound like.

When we say chase every quote, most owners picture pestering people. A salesperson ringing round, asking if you've made a decision yet. Nobody wants to be that firm.

A proper chase sounds like you on a good day. A few days after the quote, the buyer gets a short personalised video, plus the extra detail they asked about on the call. A week later, a WhatsApp voice note in your voice. Two weeks on, a follow up that reads like it came from your own phone.

Every step is built around the buyer. Professional, useful, in your voice. And the important bit: it happens every single time, whether or not anyone remembers.

Buyers don't experience that as pressure. They experience it as a company that's properly organised.

Flat revenue feels safe. Same turnover as last year, everyone still employed, a decent cash reserve and no drama.

So here's what a plateau costs. Say your firm turns over £3M. Growing 10% a year adds £300k in year one, and because it compounds, over three years the gap between growing and standing still is roughly £1.9M in revenue.

There's a quieter cost too. When you come to sell, buyers pay meaningfully more for a business that's visibly growing than one that's drifted sideways. That usually comes down to whether the sales side runs on a system or on someone's memory.

Standing still has a price. The invoice just arrives later.

There's one competitor whose name makes your jaw tighten. That feeling is useful.

It's telling you exactly where you're being out-operated, and it's almost never the product. Go back through the last three jobs they took off you.

A job you never heard about until it was finished? That's visibility. A customer of yours they nicked? That's follow up and staying in contact. A demo where they simply looked slicker? That's better education.

Every one of those points at something specific they run and you don't run yet. So write the losses down and build your own system properly, one thing at a time.

Give it 18 months and the positions can flip. They won't understand how you did it, because from the outside a good system just looks like luck.

Save this, and send it to your co-director next time that name comes up.

The work rarely goes to the cheapest quote. It goes to the last one they heard from.

Plenty of firms that have been trading for 40 or 50 years still believe a serious customer will come back on their own. They rarely do, and it's not because they didn't like your quote.

They have a job too. Your quote is one of nine tabs open in their head. They get pulled into something else, someone goes on holiday, and a month later it's slipped through the net without anyone deciding against you.

When they finally sit down to sort it, whoever followed up most recently gets the deal. Not the cheapest, not even the best. Just the firm that's there when the decision happens.

The fix is a polite, professional chase in your tone of voice that keeps going until you get a yes or a no. We've spent 3+ years building exactly that for 40+ businesses, and it's generated £10M+ for our partners so far.

Your service level isn't your average. It's your worst covered hour.

Enquiries rarely arrive at half ten on a Monday when everyone's sat there with a coffee. They turn up at the end of the day, over a bank holiday, or in the week you're away in Portugal. And that awkward hour is the one where a buyer forms his opinion of your firm.

That's no dig at your team. It's just how enquiries behave. If you've built a £2M+ business on doing things properly, it's an uncomfortable thought.

So don't test your business at a convenient moment. Send an enquiry through at 16:50 on a Friday and see what comes back.

Covering those hours is part of every system we build. We've done it for 40+ businesses over 3+ years, and it's generated £10M+ for our partners.

Somewhere in this week's enquiries is a £200k project. Can your team tell which one?

Some enquiries are tyre kickers. Some can't afford you. Some are a competitor checking your prices. And they all get the same reply, the same follow-up and the same hour of your best salesperson's afternoon.

A working system sorts them at the front door. Everyone gets a fast, polite reply that answers the questions you'd answer anyway, and asks the ones that matter. What's the project? When's it needed? What's the budget? Who signs it off?

Then it routes them. The small stuff gets handled without you. Serious buyers land in your calendar with the answers already attached, so you walk into every call knowing whether it's worth your time. In a £2M+ business, that genuinely changes a week.

"Will it sound like us?" It's the first thing owners ask about automated follow-up.

It's a fair worry. Your reputation took decades, and the last thing you want is a robot denting it in a week. Nobody wants the customer they've supplied for 20 years getting something that reads like a bank.

Done properly, it won't. Before anything goes near a prospect, we sit down with you and learn how you talk: the phrases you use, the sales calls you've taken, how formal you are with a new contact compared with a long-standing customer. Every message is written in that voice, and you approve each one before it's ever sent.

Your buyers experience you, with endless time and a perfect memory. For a £2M+ business that runs on relationships, that's the version that protects them. It's how we work with Everflow. In Samantha's words: "It feels like you are an extension of the marketing team."

Thirty years of customer relationships, and almost none of it written down.

Your best salesman retires in three years. Right now those relationships live in his head and on his phone. Who to ring, the account history, what got promised a couple of years back. Maybe some of it's in a spreadsheet.

When he goes, a chunk of your revenue goes with him. Nobody notices on his last day. They notice when the reorders slow down.

For a £2M+ business, that's a quiet risk with a deadline on it. It's fixable, but only while he's still around to fill in the gaps. Every account and every conversation captured in one place, with follow-up running on a schedule instead of on whoever has time. New starters then inherit something genuinely valuable.

Count the quotes you sent last quarter that got one chase and then silence.

Each one cost you something. A site visit, a demo, maybe an engineer's hour on the spec, the margins worked out. Then it's emailed over, someone sends a 'just checking in', and that's it. No reminder, no process.

Harvard Business Review looked at over 2,000 companies. The average reply to a new enquiry took 42 hours, and nearly a quarter never replied at all. Quotes fare worse, because everyone assumes a serious buyer will come back on their own.

They don't. Everybody's busy. They buy from whoever stayed in the conversation.

So go and count them. That number is the size of the problem, and in the 40+ businesses we've worked with it's one of the first places we look.

Your February problem probably started with a quiet week back in June.

That's when you had a spare afternoon and chased a few people. Those chases are what made autumn busy. Then autumn buries you, everyone's delivering, nothing new goes out, and February pays for it.

Real seasonality exists. But in a lot of £2M+ businesses most of the swing is just effort with a three-month delay on it, and it gets put down to the calendar.

Flexipol's pipeline used to wait for the phone to ring. We built them a system that brings enquiries in on its own, and in their first three months with us enquiries were up 60%.

The fix isn't grafting harder in the flat months. It's having something that runs whether or not you've got time that week.

Your record month might be the reason next month feels so quiet.

Best month in two years, everyone's happy, and you're quietly wondering if you can do it again. Then the phone goes quiet. The work came off a couple of one-off relationships, and everyone spent the month delivering, so nobody was filling the diary.

Sell, get busy, stop selling, go quiet, panic, sell again. Plenty of £2M+ owners have ridden that loop for years and started calling it normal.

Everflow had only ever had leads through brokers, so the flow depended on someone else. We built them their own lead channel on Meta, and it's delivered 100 leads a month for 18 consecutive months.

A record month you can't repeat isn't the win. Twelve ordinary months in a row is.

"Reply faster" is a pep talk, and it's never fixed anyone's response times.

Your team isn't lazy. Enquiries land while half of them are out on demos, in meetings or on holiday, and whoever's meant to watch the inbox is juggling four other jobs. Workload beats willpower every single time.

The firms replying in under five minutes aren't more disciplined than you. They've made it impossible to be slow. Every enquiry gets an instant reply, gets qualified, and lands in the right person's calendar. Your salespeople join the conversation warm instead of scrambling around cold.

Everflow went from paying brokers for every conversation to running their own channel on Meta, with 100 leads a month for 18 months.

Good young salespeople don't quit your business. They quit the filing cabinet.

You've seen it. A promising hire joins, lasts a few months and leaves, and everyone agrees salespeople just don't stick. But look at what they walked into. No warm enquiries, go and find your own. No system, just notes on paper. And success defined by decades-old relationships they could never copy.

The talented ones go where the pipeline is visible and there's a proper sales and marketing process, because that's where they can win and earn.

So it falls to you, the owner, to build the machine first. Enquiries flowing in automatically, follow-ups that run on their own, a CRM everyone can see. Do that and you become the firm young talent wants to join, and word gets around.

Who answered your last new enquiry, and what did they actually say?

In a lot of £2M+ businesses it's whoever's nearest. A receptionist, or a project manager in the middle of something else. They take a name and a number, say someone will get back to you, and it goes in a book.

Meanwhile that buyer is already ringing the next firm on their list.

You've trained everyone on how the work gets done. Nobody's been trained on the first 90 seconds after someone enquires, what to ask or how to book the next step. Whoever handles that opening conversation best usually wins the job. The firms that win more have a system doing the heavy lifting, so every enquiry gets qualified and followed up whoever picks up.

You spent years perfecting the work. About ten minutes on the phone decides whether you get to do it.

If you took a fortnight off tomorrow, who would close the deals?

Who knows what order things happen in when a deal comes in? What gets said, when to push and when to leave a buyer alone? If the honest answer is "I'll just do it", what you've got is a job with a few staff attached to it.

This isn't about ego, and it doesn't make you any less important. It's about what happens when you're not there.

Written down and built into a system, your sales process becomes an asset. It runs while you're on holiday, and it adds real value when you come to sell. Left in your head, it's an arrangement.

Busy isn't the same as booked, and your marketing person probably knows it.

Posts go up, the newsletter goes out, the brochure gets refreshed and the show stand gets booked. Now look at what they were given on day one. No target that means anything, no leads, nothing linking their work to an enquiry or a sale. Just "do the marketing". So they produce the only thing they can on their own, which is activity.

In a lot of £2M+ businesses the failure was baked in the day that person started, and it was never really theirs.

Fill in your own enquiry form today and start a timer. Then wait.

Do it on your phone, like a real buyer would. Make it a decent project, say £50k, with believable details. While you wait, do the same on two competitors' websites and watch who comes back first.

That's the race your buyers run every week, and most owners have never seen it from the customer's side. If your £2M+ business replies in minutes, fair play, that's rare. If it's hours or days, you've just found out where some of your enquiries have been going.

There's probably around £80k in it. The refit you priced in spring. The repeat order that stalled when the buyer changed jobs. Nobody said no. Somebody stopped replying, and your team moved on to the next new enquiry.

Those quotes aren't dead. Sometimes the buyer went elsewhere, but often they never bought at all. The project stalled, the budget moved, the person left. And they already know you. They asked you for a price. That's the warmest list a £2M+ business will ever own.

By the time most firms reply to a new enquiry, the buyer has already had two quotes.

Picture the enquiry that lands at 3pm on a Friday. Your sales manager spots it on Monday after the weekly meeting and rings at half eleven. The buyer is polite. They've moved on.

Harvard Business Review looked at lead response across more than 2,000 businesses. Reply within an hour and you're roughly seven times more likely to qualify that buyer. Reply within five minutes and that number quadruples. The average business takes 42 hours.

Speed reads as competence too. The firm that comes back in four minutes feels like the one that'll deliver on time and pick up when something goes wrong. The one that comes back on Thursday feels like the one that won't.

If you run a £2M+ business, your response time is your reputation.

What happens to your revenue if you disappear for a month?

Not a week of checking emails at breakfast and taking calls from the sun lounger. A proper month, genuinely gone.

If revenue drops, the business is you with staff attached. Every big deal still runs through your phone and your memory. If it goes up, you've been the bottleneck, which is harder to hear and more common than most owners admit.

The only good answer is about the same, with numbers you can open when you're back that show exactly what happened. Very few people running a £2M+ business can say that yet.

"Marketing doesn't work in our industry" usually comes from one bad test, years ago.

Somebody posted on LinkedIn for a while, got a few likes from your suppliers, and the phone never rang. Ever since, it's been company policy.

Look at what was actually tried. Posts and a bit of brand work, with nothing to turn a reader into an enquiry and nothing in place for when one did turn up. It was never going to produce leads. The conclusion stuck anyway, and it's been quietly costing a £2M+ business work for years.

Flexipol's directors felt the same. A food packaging manufacturer with a pipeline that mostly waited for the phone. We built the system they'd never been shown, and they had 70+ enquiries in 90 days. In Sunil's words: "We didn't even think online could be a viable channel."

You tested one weak version of marketing, once. That's a long time to keep paying for it.
